week.t: CHAPEA: four volunteers leave NASA’s 3D-printed Mars habitat after 378 days
JPL: Teghaza 001, a 4.1-billion-year-old piece of Martian crust, found in the Sahara
NEA: inter-monsoon winds setting in; haze expected to improve
Artemis III SLS core stage joins its boosters in the Vehicle Assembly Building
Lucy becomes the first spacecraft to enter Jupiter’s Trojan asteroid region
NTU and VFT open a S$15 million lab for vanadium flow batteries

tiles.cap: Artemis III’s 212-foot core stage now stands between its two boosters
tiles.nums: height of the SLS core stage now stacked between its boosters, about 65 metres
tiles.p1: NASA said on Wednesday 28 October that technicians at its Kennedy Space Center in Florida had lifted the Artemis III SLS core stage out of High Bay 2 of the Vehicle Assembly Building and set it between the twin solid rocket boosters in High Bay 3. The 212-foot stage (about 65 metres) hung from a one-of-a-kind lifting beam designed to place it onto the mobile launcher. NASA’s photos of the move and the stacking are dated Thursday 22 to Sunday 25 October, when a caption says the short stack was complete.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: this is the rocket that will carry Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio, Andre Douglas and ESA’s Luca Parmitano on the Earth-orbit docking rehearsal described in the Artemis III tile.
deep: What comes next

Once testing and checkouts are complete, the core stage and booster stack rolls out to Launch Pad 39B for a tanking test: liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen will be loaded only into the core stage, and the launch teams will run through their countdown procedures and timelines. The page gives no rollout date; NASA’s Artemis III mission page says the flight is launching in 2027.
Four engines
One of NASA’s photos, from 22 October, shows the four engines at the base of the stage, each covered in a red cap.
The mission
Artemis III will carry four astronauts in Orion atop SLS to test rendezvous and docking between Orion and commercial spacecraft from Blue Origin and SpaceX, ahead of future crewed Moon landings.

tiles.cap: After 2.2 billion miles, Lucy is the first spacecraft to reach Jupiter’s Trojans
tiles.nums: miles Lucy has travelled since its launch on 16 October 2021
tiles.p1: NASA said on Wednesday 28 October that Lucy is the first spacecraft to enter the region of the Jupiter Trojan asteroids, five years and more than 2.2 billion miles after launch. There are no well-defined boundaries in space: mission engineers know Lucy is approaching Jupiter’s Lagrange point 4 (L4) by tracking its radio signals and images of the surrounding stars. Lucy is now more than five times farther from the Sun than Earth is.
tiles.p2: Next stop: the asteroid Eurybates on 11 August 2027, less than a year away, to be observed for a few hours as Lucy flies past.
deep: Islands of stability

The Trojans share Jupiter’s orbit around the Sun, guided by the combined gravitational pull of the Sun and Jupiter. They sit in two swarms, L4 leading Jupiter and L5 trailing it, about 484 million miles from Jupiter, which is as far from Jupiter as Jupiter is from the Sun. Thousands of asteroids live in these two unexplored islands.
Lonely rocks
On average the Trojan asteroids are more than 6 million miles apart, so Lucy will see mostly empty space between its targets.
The tour

After Eurybates come Polymele in September 2027, Leucus in April 2028 and Orus in November 2028. Lucy swings back past Earth in 2030 for a third gravity assist, then reaches the binary pair Patroclus and Menoetius in March 2033.
Why primitive

NASA calls the Trojans primitive solar-system bodies. Seeing them up close should help scientists refine their theories of how the planets formed 4.5 billion years ago and how they ended up where they are.
tiles.src: NASA Lucy mission blog (Katherine Kretke, SwRI), 28 Oct 2026

tiles.cap: A rose-coloured rock found in the Sahara is a 4.1-billion-year-old piece of Mars
tiles.nums: roughly how many meteorites from Mars have been found on Earth; Teghaza 001 is among the three oldest
tiles.p1: When a rose-coloured meteorite was found in the Sahara Desert in 2022, nobody knew how old it was or where it came from. A NASA-funded team led by Yang Liu of JPL reported on Thursday 29 October in the journal Science that Teghaza 001, weighing nearly 2 pounds (800 grams), is a piece of Mars that formed more than 4.1 billion years ago, one of the three oldest Martian meteorites known. It was found on Mali’s Teghaza salt plain.
tiles.p2: “This is really our first piece of Martian crust from a part of Mars we’ve never had a sample of before,” said second author Lee Saper, who did the work at JPL and is now at NASA Ames.
deep: How you date a rock

Zircon crystals, which record clues to a rock’s formation, plus in-situ rubidium-strontium dating of single mineral grains on a surface piece smaller than a fingernail, a method pioneered by the team of Caltech co-author Francois Tissot that preserves rare samples for future work. Water on Mars altered the rock around 4.1 billion years ago, so it likely formed earlier still.
The other two

ALH84001 is nearly all one mineral and similar in age; Black Beauty formed about 2.1 billion years ago and is made of small volcanic rock fragments. Teghaza 001 has a mix of igneous minerals that record how crust formed from cooling magma and was later altered by water underground.
Where on Mars

The paper identifies 13 possible source locations on Mars that match its minerals and chemistry; its mineralogy also matches what the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter sees in the cratered southern highlands. “We’ve only scratched the surface,” said Liu. A separate paper in June, in Science Advances, detailed its water content.

tiles.cap: Four people walk out of a fake Mars on Saturday after 378 days inside
tiles.nums: days of isolation in a 3D-printed habitat at NASA’s Johnson Space Center, Houston
tiles.p1: On Saturday 31 October, Ross Elder, Ellen Ellis, James Spicer and Matthew Montgomery leave the 1,700-square-foot, 3D-printed habitat at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston where they have lived since 19 October 2025. The CHAPEA Mission 2 crew spent 378 days simulating a Mars mission: simulated spacewalks, habitat maintenance and growing plants, with communication delays, limited resources and isolation thrown in.
tiles.p2: NASA streams the exit ceremony live from 3 p.m. EDT on Saturday, which is 3 a.m. on Sunday in Singapore.
deep: What the data is for
NASA says the mission’s data could help plan lunar missions: food system design, how crews use their time, Deep Space Network bandwidth, and medical and behavioural support.
Who is there
Johnson Space Center director Vanessa Wyche and NASA astronaut Jack Hathaway will give remarks at the ceremony.
A thought to test
378 days is longer than a year: the crew went in before last Halloween and come out the day of this one.

tiles.cap: Cyclone Arnab, photographed by night from orbit, hit India’s coast at 130 km/h
tiles.nums: sustained winds when NOAA-20 captured the night image at 1:42 a.m. IST on 27 October
tiles.p1: Arnab was the first named storm of the 2026 North Indian Ocean cyclone season, forming in the Bay of Bengal on 25 October, a late start for a basin that usually produces named cyclones in April or May. The VIIRS day-night band on the NOAA-20 satellite caught it at 20:12 UTC on 26 October (1:42 a.m. IST on the 27th), when the India Meteorological Department put sustained winds at about 140 km/h. It made landfall early on 28 October on the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coast, between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam, with winds of 130 km/h.
tiles.p2: IMD’s category: a very severe cyclonic storm, similar to a Category 1 hurricane on the Saffir-Simpson scale. Tens of thousands of people were evacuated beforehand.
deep: Late this year
A basin that usually produces named cyclones in April or May got its first on 25 October. NASA’s article notes research linking the ongoing El Niño to reduced Bay of Bengal cyclone activity.
On the ground
Arnab uprooted trees, flooded crops and homes, limited fishing and disrupted transport and power.
The picture
NASA Earth Observatory image by Michala Garrison, using VIIRS day-night band data (VIIRS flies on NOAA-20); story by Adam Voiland. City lights are visible on the darkened land in the image.
tiles.src: NASA Earth Observatory, 29 Oct 2026 · India Meteorological Department
tiles.credit: Image: NASA Earth Observatory / Michala Garrison, NOAA-20 VIIRS

tiles.cap: India’s 50 m GSLV is on the pad with a satellite carrying a home-made atomic clock
tiles.nums: beyond India’s borders that NavIC signals are designed to reach
tiles.p1: ISRO posted on Wednesday 28 October that GSLV-F18, the 20th flight of its Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle, is on the Second Launch Pad at Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota, with the NVS-03 satellite on top. NVS-03 is the third satellite of the next-generation series for NavIC, India’s regional navigation system, which provides position, navigation and timing over the Indian landmass and a region extending 1500 km around it. The satellite carries an indigenous atomic clock alongside procured ones, and adds an L1 signal to the existing L5 and S signals.
tiles.p2: ISRO’s mission page said the launch was planned but gave no date or time when this was written. Watch for the result.
deep: The rocket, by the numbers

From ISRO’s mission brochure: about 50 m tall and about 420 tonnes at lift-off. The first stage is a solid-propellant stage carrying 138.2 tonnes, with four liquid strap-on boosters; the second stage is liquid-fuelled; the third is a cryogenic stage burning 14.4 tonnes of liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen.
Where it is going
Target orbit: a geosynchronous transfer orbit with a perigee of 170 km and an apogee of 37,023 km, inclined 20.75 degrees, on a launch azimuth of 106 degrees.
Why the clock matters

A navigation satellite broadcasts the time from its on-board clock; your receiver turns the arrival times of several satellites’ signals into a position. That is why the clocks are atomic, and why ISRO notes that this one is indigenous.
tiles.src: ISRO mission page and brochure, 28 Oct 2026

tiles.cap: The Sun you watch setting has already set. Light bends, and takes the fastest route
tiles.nums: how much higher the apparent Sun sits than the true Sun near the horizon, says Feynman
tiles.p1: Feynman explains Fermat’s principle with a rescue. Someone has fallen out of a boat; you are on land, and you can run faster than you can swim. Do you go in a straight line? “Yes, no doubt!” says Feynman, then thinks again: it pays to run a little further along the land to shorten the swim. Light does the same. Fermat proposed in about 1650 that of all the possible paths between two points, light takes the one that needs the shortest time, and from that one idea come both the law of reflection and Snell’s law of refraction.
tiles.p2: Test tonight: when you see the Sun setting, it is already well below the horizon. The atmosphere, thin at the top and dense at the bottom, curves the light so the apparent Sun is higher than the true Sun by about half a degree.
deep: The water rule

Snell’s law: the sine of the angle in air equals a constant times the sine of the angle in water, and for water that constant n is approximately 1.33. Ptolemy had tabulated the bending long before: 10 degrees in air becomes 8 in water, 50 becomes 35, 80 becomes 50.
What least time predicts

If light takes the shortest-time path, the ratio of the sines must equal the ratio of the speeds, so light must travel slower in water than in air, by the factor n. Snell’s law alone never said that; the least-time idea did, and measurement agrees.
The mirage

On a hot road the air just above the surface is hotter and thinner than the cooler air higher up, and it slows light less, so light from the sky curves up into your eye. You see “water” on the road; when you get there it is as dry as the desert. What you saw was sky light “reflected” on the road.
Try it
Stand a pencil or spoon in a glass of water and look from the side. The kink at the surface is refraction, the bending Snell measured and least time explains.
tiles.src: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. I, Ch. 26 (Caltech)

tiles.cap: Bend dry spaghetti and it almost never breaks in two. Feynman puzzled over it. Twist first
tiles.nums: pieces a bent strand of dry spaghetti almost always snaps into
tiles.p1: Hold a strand of dry spaghetti by both ends and bend it until it breaks. You will almost never get two pieces: it snaps into three or more. Physicists, Richard Feynman among them, tried to work out why. The answer came in 2005 from Basile Audoly and Sébastien Neukirch at the University of Paris 6: after the first break, bending waves run along the strand, raise its curvature, and trigger an avalanche of new breaks, each sending out more waves.
tiles.p2: In 2018 Ronald Heisser and Vishal Patil at MIT found the trick: twist the strand hard first, then bend it slowly, and it breaks into two.
deep: Why twist works
Patil’s model says the first break releases twisting (torsional) waves that travel faster than the bending waves and carry away the energy that would otherwise have gone into further breaks.
Try it at the kitchen table
Bend a strand and count the pieces; repeat a few times. Then twist a fresh strand as far as you can and bend it slowly. Count again.
Beyond pasta

Physics World notes the research could lead to new ways of using twist to prevent fractures in rod-like materials such as multifibre structures and nanotubes, and help explain natural structures such as microtubules inside living cells.

tiles.cap: A phone whose camera pops out on a titanium robot arm and spins 360° in a second
tiles.nums: machining precision Honor claims for the titanium gimbal; the gap where it rotates is 0.4 mm
tiles.p1: The Honor Robot Phone, in TIME’s Best Inventions of 2026, carries its 200-megapixel main camera on a palm-sized robotic arm with four degrees of freedom: pan, tilt, roll and flip. On command it swivels out of the back of the phone and AI software tracks whatever it is pointed at, including you in selfie mode; when it is done, the arm folds flat into the camera panel. Honor says it developed its own micromotor and packed in more than 100 new components. The gimbal motor weighs 2.6 g, is titanium alloy, and turns the camera at up to 360 degrees per second.
tiles.p2: What reviewers found wrong: Tom’s Guide’s John Velasco found the gimbal cannot rotate for true vertical video, it just crops the centre; he was leery about low light with a 1/1.28-inch sensor, worried about the moving parts in a drop, found it hefty at 8.75 ounces (an iPhone 17 Pro is 7.27), and it is not coming to the US.
deep: Inside the arm

The flip motor is made from a 2100 MPa steel Honor calls shield steel, with 43 components in a 0.5 cubic centimetre space and a five-speed transmission. Torque density is quoted at up to 120 newton-metres per litre, with a rare-earth NdFeB core.
The cameras

Main: 200 MP on a 1/1.28-inch sensor, f/1.6, with optical and 3-axis mechanical stabilisation. Periscope telephoto: 200 MP, 1/1.4-inch, 2.7x optical zoom. Ultra-wide: 50 MP with a 122-degree field of view. Video up to 4K at 120 frames per second through Honor’s H1 image chip.
The rest of the phone

Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 on a 3 nm process, a 6.31-inch OLED that peaks at 6,800 nits, and a 7,060 mAh silicon-carbon battery with 120 W wired and 50 W wireless charging. Announced in China on 12 August 2026 at RMB 9,999 and RMB 12,999, with sales from 18 August.
A number to doubt
Velasco’s spec table lists 25 W wired charging; Honor’s own pages say 120 W. They cannot both be right, and a charging claim is exactly the kind of number to time with a stopwatch.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 · Honor product and launch pages · Tom’s Guide, 12 Aug 2026

tiles.cap: Woodlands hit 36.1 °C on 23 October. Now the winds go slack, and the haze should ease
tiles.nums: highest daily maximum of the fortnight, recorded at Woodlands on 23 October 2026
tiles.p1: The Meteorological Service Singapore said on Thursday 29 October that the Southwest Monsoon is weakening and inter-monsoon conditions are setting in. The second half of October brought winds mostly from the southeast or southwest, which carried smoke haze to Singapore: air quality reached Unhealthy levels on seven days and Very Unhealthy on three between 16 and 28 October. The inter-monsoon period brings light and variable winds instead, so smoke haze is less likely to reach Singapore and the haze situation is expected to improve.
tiles.p2: Also in the review: daily maximums above 34 °C on most days, and most of the island had below-average rain. Tanjong Katong was 72 per cent below average while Punggol was 24 per cent above.
deep: The first half of November

Moderate to heavy thundery showers in the afternoon on most days, sometimes into the evening; total rainfall forecast slightly above average; daily maximums between 33 and 35 °C on most days, with a few days slightly above 35.
The wettest spot
The highest daily rainfall of the fortnight was 81.0 mm at Tuas South on 21 October.
Across the water

NEA’s regional page on Thursday evening: scattered hotspots mainly in southern Kalimantan, moderate to dense smoke plumes over southern and eastern Kalimantan, and a few air quality stations in Sumatra and Kalimantan reporting Unhealthy levels. Extensive cloud cover hid the full picture.
Yesterday’s forecast
NEA’s PSI forecast for Thursday 29 October was 60 to 90, Moderate. At 5 pm on Wednesday the 24-hour PSI was 66 to 78.

tiles.cap: A battery that keeps its energy in two tanks of non-flammable liquid: NTU’s S$15m lab
tiles.nums: size of the four-year NTU–VFT joint lab announced on Tuesday 27 October
tiles.p1: NTU’s Energy Research Institute (ERI@N) and VFT, an NTU spin-off founded in 2018, have launched a S$15 million joint research laboratory, NTU said on Tuesday 27 October, to develop vanadium redox flow batteries for the power grid. Unlike lithium-ion batteries, which store energy inside the cells, a flow battery stores it in liquid electrolytes held in external tanks; the liquids are water-based and non-flammable, which NTU says significantly reduces the risk of battery fires.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: as grids add more intermittent solar and wind, they need a safe way to store electricity when generation is high and release it when renewable output falls or demand rises.
deep: What they will work on
Better battery stacks and cooling, recovering and recycling the vanadium, power conversion efficiency, and AI-based fault detection and maintenance prediction.
Who

Professor Madhavi Srinivasan, executive director of ERI@N: “As the global energy transition accelerates, safe and efficient energy storage will become increasingly important to keeping electricity supplies stable and reliable.” VFT’s chief executive, Dr Vidal Bharath, says the challenge is no longer simply generating more renewable energy but finding safe, reliable and affordable ways to store it for when generation falls or demand rises.
The spin-off

VFT is built on technology developed at ERI@N and raised US$20.5 million in 2025 to expand manufacturing. The lab was launched at the Asia Clean Energy Summit during Singapore International Energy Week 2026 and is supported under the Research, Innovation and Enterprise 2025 plans.

tiles.cap: Roll a sheet of paper into a tube and you can see straight through your own hand
tiles.nums: length of the tube: one A4 sheet rolled lengthwise, about 1.25 cm across
tiles.p1: Roll a sheet of A4 paper lengthwise into a tube about 28 cm long and 1.25 cm in diameter, and tape it so it stays rolled. Hold it to your right eye with your right hand and look through it, keeping both eyes open. Now bring your left hand up, fingers pointing up and palm facing you, against the left side of the tube about halfway along. Your hand appears to have a hole in it.
tiles.p2: Swap: tube in the left hand to the left eye, right palm against it. Some people find the effect stronger one way round.
deep: What is going on
One of your eyes sees a hole, the other sees a hand. Your eyes and brain add the two images together and build a hand with a hole in it.
Your dominant eye

The effect is often stronger with one eye because one eye is likely dominant: your brain has a slight preference for its signal, much as you prefer one hand, though eye and hand preference do not have to match.
Find yours

Tear a coin-sized hole in a piece of paper, pick a distant object and look at it through the hole. Slowly bring the paper to your face while keeping the object in view. The eye the hole ends up against is your dominant eye. Exploratorium adds that top baseball hitters often don’t have a dominant eye.
Circle or oval

Make a second tube and squash it into a flat oval. Look through the round tube with one eye and the oval with the other at a white wall, and angle them so the two spots overlap. Most people see one shape, the one from the dominant eye; some see both overlapped.
tiles.src: Exploratorium Science Snacks: Hole in Your Hand · Circles or Ovals

tiles.p1: Behavioural scientist Benjamin Lira Luttges at Penn put it in six words. Hand the boring, repetitive stuff to the machine. Keep for yourself anything you want to become good at, and anything you enjoy. His colleague Trent Cash at Waterloo adds the mechanism: if we offload a specific skill to AI, we are probably not going to retain that skill particularly well.
tiles.p2: Why it is not scary: Cash also says humans are resilient and AI will not turn our brains to mush. It is a choice, made daily.
deep: The doctors who forgot
Doctors used an AI tool for three months to spot growths during colonoscopies. When it was switched off, they found fewer than before. Three months was enough for the skill to fade.
The readers who gave up

People who worked through SAT reading questions with AI help were more likely to skip questions once the help was removed. The researchers called that particularly concerning, because sticking with a hard question is itself the skill.
Your list
Write down three skills you want to be yours at 20. Those never get outsourced. Everything else is fair game.
tiles.src: Science News Explores · Cash et al. 2026 · Lira Luttges et al. 2026

tiles.cap: Madagascar’s giant bats, wingspan up to 1.5 m, are shrinking. Museum skulls told the story
tiles.nums: how much longer pre-1980s flying-fox skulls were than later ones, about 6 per cent
tiles.p1: The Madagascan flying fox, Pteropus rufus, is among the world’s biggest bats; fruit bats like it have wingspans of up to a metre and a half. Emily Cornelius Ruhs of Chicago’s Field Museum noticed that preserved specimens looked larger than bats caught today. With Steven Goodman she measured 12 skull and tooth features on 121 specimens from nine museums, collected over more than 150 years. Skulls from before the 1980s were 3.6 millimetres, about 6 per cent, longer than those collected after.
tiles.p2: Published Thursday 29 October in the Journal of Mammalogy. The timing of the shrink matches the rise of commercial bat hunting, which may take the biggest animals first; climate change and habitat loss are other possible causes.
deep: A population in trouble

Estimated at 300,000 in the early 2000s, the population is now down by about two-thirds. “Bats are eaten in Madagascar in certain villages and cultures,” says Ruhs; the question she raises is how to overcome the needs of the people who live there.
Why size matters

Smaller bodies could affect how the species copes with environmental, climate or disease stress. Emma Stone of the University of Bath: “Species are specifically adapted to their environments and adaptation takes place over thousands of years.”
Museums as time machines
Specimens collected over more than 150 years let a bat from 1948 sit next to one from 1995 and tell a story that no single field trip could.
tiles.src: Science News, 29 Oct 2026 (Jake Buehler) · Ruhs & Goodman, Journal of Mammalogy

tiles.cap: A spider turns liquid “dope” into thread tougher than Kevlar in milliseconds. Here’s how
tiles.nums: types of silk spiders can spin; one spider often makes several
tiles.p1: Spider silk is tougher than Kevlar and stronger than steel, yet nobody has matched it, partly because nobody knew how a spider turns a soup of proteins into a fibre within milliseconds. Gregory Holland’s team at San Diego State University used NMR, nuclear magnetic resonance, on liquid silk dope from black widows and mapped the steps, Quanta Magazine reported on Wednesday 28 October. The key is a condensate: phosphate triggers two amino acids, arginine and tyrosine, to interact, pushing water out and forming a denser, gel-like state whose sticky interaction persists into the finished fibre.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: silkworms have been farmed for more than 4,000 years, but spiders eat each other, so each needs its own container, and it would take around a million of them to make one silk shirt. Lab-made spider silk is still weaker than the real thing.
deep: Holy grail

Holland calls mapping the molecular steps from dope to fibre “really the holy grail”. The silk proteins, later named spidroins, were identified in 1907. Packages of black widows arrived every few months through 2023 and 2024; six times over two weeks, graduate student Hannah Johnson put on two pairs of protective gloves to silk them.
One protein, two states

Kevin Chalek, then a postdoc in the lab: “These are the same protein, so how can they be so different?” Simulations suggest arginine and tyrosine sit at the bends of beta sheets, guiding the proteins into their final structure.
Not just spiders

Condensates have been observed for more than a century: lab-made spidroins formed liquid-like globs in 2007, condensates turned up in worm eggs in 2009, and in 2020 Keiji Numata proposed that spider silk passes through a condensate phase. “It’s becoming clear that condensates are a common strategy that’s being used across a range of different organisms,” says Matthew Harrington of McGill. Daiwen Yang of NUS, not involved, calls the findings direct evidence.
tiles.src: Quanta Magazine, 28 Oct 2026 (Yasemin Saplakoglu) · Holland lab, PNAS

tiles.cap: Artemis III: four astronauts, two Moon landers, one docking rehearsal in Earth orbit
tiles.nums: planned length of the 2027 Artemis III mission in low Earth orbit
tiles.p1: NASA set out on Friday 23 October how Artemis III will fly. Launching in 2027, it will send NASA astronauts Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio and Andre Douglas and ESA astronaut Luca Parmitano into low Earth orbit aboard Orion, launched on the SLS rocket from Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Over a planned 14 days they will rendezvous and dock with test versions of two Moon landers: Blue Origin’s Blue Moon Mark 2 and SpaceX’s Starship Version 3.
tiles.p2: Why Earth orbit first: everything learned here, says Artemis program manager Jeremy Parsons, gets NASA closer to landing on the Moon in 2028, when Artemis astronauts are due to begin landing near the Moon’s South Pole.
deep: The order of events

Blue Origin goes first, launching a Blue Moon Mark 2 test article into a circular low Earth orbit; it can stay up for as long as 30 days, which gives the schedule room. Orion follows and docks, and the astronauts spend about two days inside the Blue Moon test article checking the cabin environment, controls and life-support systems first-hand.
Then Starship
SpaceX launches a Starship Version 3 test article from Florida. Orion will rendezvous and dock with it in a test expected to last up to two hours. The crew will not go inside Starship on this flight.
Spare days

Orion then has up to five more days in orbit for checks of the Orion Crew Survival System suits and docking-sensor tests, a cellular biology experiment, and trials of ways to bring Moon samples back to Earth. Splashdown is in the Pacific Ocean, off the coast of California.
Three at once

“We’re launching three spacecraft on three different rockets and testing how they operate together,” said Parsons in NASA’s account of the plan. He presented it at a Kennedy briefing on Friday with NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and Associate Administrator Amit Kshatriya. Artemis IV is planned as the first Artemis mission on the lunar surface.
